 Four numbers per trial tool: invocation count by session class (is anyone using it, and who), denial rate by code (schema friction), approval-stamp rate (tier calibration), and journal-sample disagreement rate (planner's stated reason versus gate's classification, sampled twenty calls). Publish them in the promotion review doc beside the schema diff; a tool whose numbers nobody reads gets default sunset at six months, which converts registry entropy into scheduled arithmetic -- the same trick the config orphan reviews use, and for the same reason: entropy's only reliable opponent is a calendar with an owner. 

 
 Can stages be compressed for urgent tools? 
 Stages 1-2 never (schema and classification are the load-bearing walls); stage 3 can compress to 72 hours with doubled journal sampling for internal-curated tools, never for open-web-sourced ones. The compression rule is written in the registry policy so urgency debates happen once, at policy time, rather than per tool at 5 p.m. on a deadline day. 
 
 
 How do wrappers fit the staged path? 
 Wrappers (implementations that make hidden writes explicit, bound unbounded parameters, or add approval prompts) are stage-2 outputs: the wrapper is the tool, the wrapped binary is its dependency, and the registry row cites both. Reviewing wrappers means reviewing the delta they add -- usually under two hundred lines -- which is why wrapper-first onboarding is often faster than arguing with an upstream tool's actual behavior. 
 
 
 What kills a tool fastest post-promotion? 

 Keep one paragraph per tool beside its registry row -- a biography: why it arrived, what it replaced, what it was expected to change. Biographies make sunset reviews short and re-adoption decisions informed; their absence is felt only during the conversation that needs them most, which is always the one running against an incident timer. 
 


## Should I Log Every Agent Action? What Goes in the Journal?
https://codesbyfebin.github.io/blog/ai-infra/log-every-agent-action/
Scope: Adapted from supplied workspace article draft


 Journal schema: seven fields, zero opinions 
 
  {"ts":"2026-02-11T03:14:07Z","sess":"S-9f2","tool":"fs_write",
 "args":{"sha":"3f9c…","bytes":4127,"scope":"sess-paths"},
 "gate":"execute","reason":"save draft per user request #3",
 "dur_ms":12,"outcome":"ok"}  
 Args as hash plus size: forensics needs identity, privacy needs restraint, and the raw args live behind access control. 
 
 Hash-and-size args keep the journal readable at scale and privacy-defensible by default; full args stay in a tier-2 store with access logging, opened only under incident review policy. The  reason  field is the planner's own text captured at decision time -- post-hoc summaries lie, contemporaneous quotes do not, and the gap between reason and outcome is where misbehavior becomes visible: a write justified by "user asked" with no user turn in the session transcript is an injection signature, detectable by joining two logs nobody thought to join. 

 The three disciplines the journal enables 
 
  Forensics : session replay as a query (all calls, verdicts, reasons in order); incident timelines assembled in minutes instead of archaeology weeks. 
  Calibration : denial histograms per tool and class, approval-stamp rates, reason-versus-classification disagreement sampling -- the measurement loop from the  onboarding Q&A  runs entirely off journal aggregates. 
  Trust accounting : monthly per-session summaries (calls by class, writes by scope tier, denials) published to the humans who own the agent; trust that is reported survives, trust that is assumed expires at the first incident. 
 

 Journal operations: append-only, shipped, sampled 
 Append-only with hash-chaining (each entry references the previous hash) makes silent edits detectable -- the integrity trick from the federation manifests, applied to logs; ship to the backup target nightly because local journals die with local disks per the  offsite guide ; retain hot ninety days, cold per policy with the access log of every cold open. Sample weekly: twenty random write-class entries read by a human comparing reason to outcome -- the sample is cheap, and the knowledge that a sample exists changes how everyone writes reasons, which is the cheapest behavioral control in the entire stack. 

 Alerts off the journal, not off the agent 
 Four standing alerts: denial-code two-sigma spikes (schema confusion or capability gap), write-scope tier escalation (a session touching a higher tier than its capability row -- always an incident or a taxonomy bug), reason-absence on write-class calls (planner invoking without traceable justification), and journal-gap detection (hash-chain discontinuity or shipping failure). Each alert names an owner in the registry beside the tool; unowned alerts are wallpaper, and wallpaper is how journals become compliance artifacts instead of instruments -- the difference between a cockpit and a museum, which is the difference this entire cluster keeps drawing between systems that watch and systems that merely record. 





## Which Local Models Are Actually Good for Coding?
https://codesbyfebin.github.io/blog/ai-infra/local-models-for-coding/
Scope: Adapted from supplied workspace article draft


 The three tiers, with honest job descriptions 
 
  Completion tier (7-8B coder, Q8) : line and block completion, test boilerplate, regex-and-CSV chores. Fast on CPU-plus-small-GPU boxes; errors are local and obvious; the tier where local models beat cloud latency for keystroke-coupled work. 
  Conversation tier (13-14B, Q4-Q6) : explain this module, draft this function, convert this pattern; long-context reads of single files plus neighbors. Quality holds when context stays under ~8k of relevant code -- retrieval discipline matters more than model size here, per the RAG guide's chunking rules applied to repositories. 
  Architecture tier (30B+, Q4 where memory allows) : cross-module refactoring proposals, migration planning, review commentary. Useful as a senior-ish second reader whose suggestions compile-check before belief; never as an authority, per the verification habits below. 
 

 The four-test audition before adoption 
 
  FIM discipline : give prefix and suffix of a real function; a coding-capable model respects the suffix boundary instead of rewriting past it. 
  Diff format : request changes as unified diff on a 300-line file; count malformed hunks across ten runs -- patch-parseable output is the gate for editor integration. 
  Long-context honesty : embed the question's answer deep in an 8k-token file with two decoys; models that cite the decoy confidently fail, regardless of benchmark fame. 
  Tool-call restraint : in an agent harness, does the model call search/read tools when context lacks the answer, or hallucinate from priors? Restraint under uncertainty is the trait that predicts safe agent behavior, and it is measurable in an evening. 
 


 Workflow integration that survives contact 
 Editor completion from tier one with a 200 ms debounce and local-only routing (the sensitive-mode toggle from the  paste-safety guide ); chat and review from tier two behind the gateway with citations-to-file-paths enforced in the prompt; architecture drafts from tier three exported as markdown for human editing, never piped into apply-patch tooling. Compile-and-test feedback loops close the quality gap materially: models whose patches run your test suite improve in effective correctness far beyond their raw benchmark delta, because the suite is a verifier the model cannot charm -- the proof cluster's philosophy arriving in software engineering clothes, verification over vibes. 

 Where local coding models still lose, named plainly 





## Q4 vs Q8 Quantization: What Do I Actually Lose?
https://codesbyfebin.github.io/blog/ai-infra/q4-vs-q8-quantization/
Scope: Adapted from supplied workspace article draft


 The deltas, by task family 
 
   Task family  Q4_K_M vs FP16  Q8_0 vs FP16  Q4 vs Q8 gap   
 
  Summarization  -1.2%  -0.4%  within rubric noise  
  Extraction / JSON  -2.1%  -0.8%  small but visible at scale  
  Code completion  -3.4%  -1.2%  measurable in compile-pass rate  
  Multi-hop reasoning  -5.8%  -2.0%  the gap that bites  
  Exact recall from context  -8.3%  -3.1%  largest; test explicitly  
 
 


 Why the loss lands where it lands 
 Quantization error is not uniform noise: importance-aware schemes protect salient channels, so common patterns survive while rare, precise weight configurations -- exactly what exact-recall and long-chain composition depend on -- absorb the rounding. The behavioral signature follows: fluency and gist hold (distribution-typical outputs), precision tails suffer (distribution-atypical outputs). This is also why vibe checks mislead: ten casual prompts feel identical across quants while your twentieth, hardest workflow degrades; harnesses exist because humans sample the easy tail by instinct. The  quantization explainer  carries the format-level mechanics; this page prices the consequences. 

 Speed and memory: what you buy with the loss 


 The twenty-minute decision protocol 
 
 Pull 50 real requests from your gateway journal or workflow logs (the  gateway piece  makes this a query, not a project). 
 Score Q8 as baseline with an automatic metric plus ten human-rubric samples. 
 Score Q4_K_M identically; compute per-family deltas against the table above as sanity, not substitute. 
 Decide per deployment slot: daily-driver chat and drafting tolerate Q4; recall- or code-critical slots get Q8 if memory allows; pin whichever artifact hash the decision produced. 
 
 Twenty minutes, two numbers, one pinned hash -- and the decision re-runs itself whenever models or runtimes upgrade, because the request corpus lives in-repo beside the scoring script. Teams that skip the protocol do not skip the decision; they make it by folklore, and folklore's quantization opinions are usually somebody's GPU vendor's marketing wearing a benchmark's costume. 





## Does a Local LLM Hallucinate More Than a Cloud One?
https://codesbyfebin.github.io/blog/ai-infra/local-llm-hallucinates-more/
Scope: Adapted from supplied workspace article draft


 The variables that actually move hallucination 
 
  Scale and training mix : the dominant terms; frontier cloud models lead here, and no deployment choice changes it. 

  Context discipline : over-long or contradictory context raises confabulation in every model class; retrieval quality (the RAG guide's eval loop) moves local hallucination more than any server decision. 
  Sampling settings : temperature and top-p drifts affect local and cloud equally; pinned configs in your gateway make this a controlled variable instead of folklore. 
 

 Measuring your own rate, in one evening 


 Controls that beat deployment-location anxiety 
 
  Citation enforcement  on fact-mode prompts, with post-processing that flags uncited factual claims (the RAG guide's trust architecture). 
  Refusal training by prompt contract : explicit "say you cannot verify" instructions measurably convert hallucinations into refusals at small quality cost -- refusals are recoverable errors; confabulations are not. 
  Verification gates for consequential outputs : code goes to compilers and tests, numbers to recomputation, citations to resolver lookups -- machines checking machines, the portfolio's standing pattern from proofs to patches. 
  Tier routing : recall-heavy and citation-bearing workloads to Q8-or-cloud slots; drafting and transformation to Q4 local; the gateway's alias table makes tiering invisible to clients. 
 

 The honest summary for decision-makers 


 
 Does longer context increase local hallucination more than cloud? 
 Context-length sensitivity scales with model class, not hosting: small models degrade faster past their trained context sweet spot, and KV quantization (a local memory-saving habit) adds a second degradation source at long contexts. Keep long-context slots at Q8 KV or above, and chunk-and-retrieve instead of pasting corpora -- the same advice the RAG and VRAM guides give from their own angles, converging because the physics is shared. 
 
 
 Can self-consistency sampling fix local hallucination cheaply? 
 Partially and measurably: majority-vote over 5 samples cuts trap-class hallucination roughly in half at 5x compute -- affordable on CPU batches overnight, painful interactively. Use it for offline artifacts (summaries, extractions into records) where latency is free, and spend interactive budget on retrieval and citations instead; sampling tricks are batch economics, not conversation economics. 
 
 
 Should user-facing UIs disclose local model use? 
 Yes, plainly: a one-line model-and-tier indicator per response (name, quant, routing exception if any) matches the citation philosophy and costs nothing. Disclosure converts user calibration from guesswork into habit -- calibrated users report fewer trust incidents and file better feedback, and better feedback is the eval set's most renewable source, closing the loop between honesty and quality in a way no benchmark purchase can. 
 


## How Should I Cache LLM Responses Without Stale Answers?
https://codesbyfebin.github.io/blog/ai-infra/cache-llm-responses/
Scope: Adapted from supplied workspace article draft


 The three layers, and what each buys 
 
  Exact-match : key = sha256(model-id + version + serialized prompt + sampling params + system text); hits are free latency and free watts; TTLs by volatility class (facts: hours; drafts: minutes; codegen: hours with invalidation on dependency hashes where available). 
  Prefix/prompt-cache : provider- or runtime-level reuse of KV for shared system-plus-context prefixes; pays on long-context RAG and agent loops where the prefix dwarfs the turn -- the runtime-side cousin of exact-match, and the reason long-context costs fall non-linearly with conversation length. 
  Artifact cache : embeddings per chunk hash (the RAG ingest dedupe from the  RAG guide ), summaries per source-hash, extractions per document-hash; the highest-leverage layer because artifacts outlive conversations and recompute costs dominate ingest budgets. 
 

 Correctness: the four invalidation laws 
 Cache entries are promises that the world has not changed; four changes break the promise and must invalidate or version: model or weight change (version in key, old entries age out), sampling parameter change (in key), context-affecting data change (artifact layers hash the source; exact-match cannot know -- accept staleness per TTL or add dependency hashes), and access-tier change (never cache across tiers: a cached answer computed with tier-A retrieval served to tier-B sessions is an authorization bug wearing a performance feature's clothing, the retrieval-authorization rule from the RAG guide restated at cache altitude). 

 Operations: hit rates, poisoning, and the watts ledger 


 When not to cache 
 Personalized generation where the prompt embeds session-private state you cannot key safely; agentic planning turns where repetition is itself the signal (caching a planner's exploratory calls hides loops you need to see in journals); and any response class under active evaluation (A/B prompts, regression suites -- cached answers make benchmark runs measure the cache). The rule of thumb: cache where repetition means redundancy; skip where repetition means information, because the journal's loop-detection and your eval harness both read the uncached stream, and a cache that starves them is a performance feature eating your instruments. 




## Can AI Agents Verify Their Own Actions With Proofs?
https://codesbyfebin.github.io/blog/ai-infra/agents-verify-own-actions/
Scope: Adapted from supplied workspace article draft


 What machines can check about an agent's own work 
 
  Execution integrity : zkVM proofs that a declared program ran on declared inputs producing declared outputs -- the  rust-stark-zkvm  pattern applied to agent batch steps, turning "I processed the dataset" into a verifiable receipt. 
  Structural invariants : schemas validate, types compile, tests pass, lints clean -- compilers and suites as the oldest verification gates in the building, still the highest-yield. 
  Journal integrity : hash-chained logs where each entry references its predecessor; tampering breaks the chain, per the  journaling guide . 
  Policy conformance : gate verdicts recorded beside actions; a conformance checker replays sessions against policy and flags any action lacking its grant -- policy as testable specification, the APG-1 discipline. 
 

 What stays human, forever 
 Intent and proportionality: the agent deleted exactly the files policy allowed -- correctly, catastrophically wrong anyway. Premise truth: the task said "the report is outdated" and the agent verified every step of replacing it, none of the premise. Relevance and taste: outputs that satisfy the letter while missing the point. These are judgment calls by definition, and the mature design routes them to approval gates with context (the diff, the premise sources, the alternatives considered) rather than pretending verification covers them. The  deletion-prevention guide 's confirmation gates are exactly this layer: machines bound the blast radius; humans own the meaning. 

 Receipt-carrying actions: the pattern in production 
 
  {"action":"transform_dataset","tool":"batch_etl",
 "receipt":{"zkvm_proof":"sha256:8f3a…","vkey":"sha256:21c9…",
            "inputs_hash":"sha256:…","outputs_hash":"sha256:…",
            "policy_grant":"G-114","journal_prev":"sha256:…"}}  
 Every consequential action leaves with a verifiable envelope: proof, pins, grant, chain link. 
 


 The research edge: what self-verification may yet eat 




 
 Is self-verification enough for regulated workflows? 
 It is necessary and insufficient: regulators ask for accountability structures (owners, approvals, retention), not just correctness artifacts. Receipts satisfy the integrity column of an audit brilliantly; the authority column still needs named humans at gates and documented delegation chains. Estates that present proofs as compliance substitutes learn the distinction during the audit; estates that present proofs inside a governance story learn nothing, because the audit simply agrees -- which is the entire goal. 
 


## Authentication and identity boundaries in a full-stack app
https://codesbyfebin.github.io/blog/grok-build/building-secure-authentication-oauth-identity/
Scope: New adaptation of supplied Grok platform documentation: auth/references/session-ui.md
Start with the session state
A session lookup has at least three useful outcomes: unresolved, authenticated, and unauthenticated. A null user value may represent either loading or a completed lookup that found no session. Redirecting on null alone can bounce an authenticated visitor during a reload. The supplied template distinguishes user data from a pending flag; preserve that distinction in any adaptation.

UI gates and authorization
An interface gate controls what the visitor sees. It does not authorize a server operation. Check the resolved identity and resource ownership inside the operation that reads or changes protected data. Do not trust a user identifier supplied in a request body as the caller identity. Rendering a signed-in component is useful for presentation, but a direct request must cross the same authorization boundary.

Avoid authentication flicker
Wait until the session check finishes before rendering a sign-in call to action. A loading skeleton or neutral state can communicate progress without falsely declaring that the user is signed out. A data-source outage should have its own error state; it should not be converted into a login requirement merely because the fetch failed.

OAuth and account ownership
OAuth redirects, callback verification, cookies, and session creation belong to the chosen identity implementation. Review its current official documentation before copying a template helper. The supplied platform documentation describes platform-managed identity behavior; those helpers are not a portable OAuth server and are not installed by this static portfolio.

Checks before release
Test a signed-out visitor, a valid session, an expired session, and a delayed session lookup. Then issue a direct request for another user's resource. Confirm that the operation rejects the request even if the client interface is bypassed. Keep test credentials synthetic and redact tokens from failure output.

Scope of the example
This article explains the supplied template's boundaries. It does not claim that this portfolio has authentication or that an OAuth integration was executed. The portfolio is static; authentication belongs in a separate application with a reviewed backend.

## PostgreSQL persistence and local preview boundaries
https://codesbyfebin.github.io/blog/grok-build/serverless-postgresql-database-design-scale/
Scope: New adaptation of supplied Grok platform documentation: neon/SKILL.md
Choose persistence deliberately
The supplied template offers PostgreSQL-backed persistence with a local embedded fallback. A browser-local preference does not need a shared database. Records that must survive across devices or be shared between users do. Make that requirement explicit before introducing migrations and operational dependencies.

Preview is a different environment
The local PGLite fallback can make a preview work without a provisioned remote database. That is useful for development, but successful preview writes do not establish deployed durability. Record which database source the application is using, and confirm that a production restart preserves a synthetic record.

Keep access on the server
The supplied database helper belongs in server functions or server loaders. A database connection string is a server credential and should not appear in client bundles or API responses. Put schema changes in migrations with a deliberate order, and keep query values parameterized rather than building SQL by concatenating user input.

Ownership is part of the query
For user-owned records, obtain the caller identity from the session and enforce it in reads and writes. A correctly parameterized query can still disclose another user's data when the ownership condition is absent. Test that a guessed resource identifier cannot cross the tenant boundary.

Plan failure and recovery
Connection availability, migration compatibility, and backup restoration are separate concerns. An application that can write one row may still fail during a dependency outage or upgrade. Test an unavailable database and preserve an explicit error state. Restore a backup into an isolated instance before describing the installation as recoverable.

Validate the deployed mode
Use synthetic data to test write, read, restart, and read again. Inspect the documented provisioning switch in the actual platform instead of assuming the presence of migration files selects the correct backend. The static portfolio includes no database; this guide is an adaptation of the supplied platform documentation.

## WebRTC data channels and the trust boundary of peer-to-peer play
https://codesbyfebin.github.io/blog/grok-build/webrtc-peer-to-peer-multiplayer/
Scope: New adaptation of supplied Grok platform documentation: multiplayer-p2p/SKILL.md
Separate signaling from gameplay
WebRTC peers exchange connection information through signaling, then establish a data channel under the network conditions available to them. The supplied template describes a mesh primitive and a small signaling route to implement. A signaling endpoint does not itself provide authoritative game-state validation.

Count the connections
In a full mesh, each participant connects to every other participant. The number of peer pairs is n times n minus one divided by two: four participants need six pairs, while eight need twenty-eight. Room size affects connection management and upload demand. Measure the actual payload rate before choosing a capacity limit.

Choose the authority model
A peer can modify its client and send false positions or scores. Cooperative play among known participants has different requirements from competitive ranking. If the product requires trusted results, define an authoritative validation path rather than accepting peer messages as proof of fair play.

Make connection failures visible
NAT and firewall behavior can prevent direct connectivity. Applications may require relay infrastructure depending on their design. The supplied template's failure state should be surfaced per peer; do not leave a participant in a permanent connecting state. This article makes no measured latency or connection-success claim.

Handle lifecycle and privacy
Leaving a room should close data channels, release listeners, and stop retry activity. Reconnect behavior needs stable participant identity and a clear rule for stale messages. Peer connectivity can expose network information to participants, so explain the product's privacy boundary before matchmaking with strangers.

Test a small room
Connect two test clients, send ordered state updates, disconnect one participant, and inspect recovery. Repeat with a third participant and verify that a departing peer does not leave ghost state. Introduce a forged score message to confirm that the chosen authority model handles it as intended. These are proposed checks, not reported results.

## Browser game loops: timing, input, and explicit state
https://codesbyfebin.github.io/blog/grok-build/browser-game-loop-and-state/
Scope: New adaptation of supplied Grok platform documentation: building-games/SKILL.md
Separate simulation from rendering
A game loop samples input, advances state, and renders the current view. These responsibilities can be implemented together initially, but their boundaries matter during testing. Rendering frequency may vary with device load or a background tab; a simulation should not assume every frame has the same duration.

Make the state machine visible
Use explicit states such as ready, playing, paused, and finished. Define which actions are accepted in each state. Restart should initialize the same resources and values as a fresh start. A collection of loosely related boolean flags can allow impossible combinations that become difficult to reproduce.

Input has a lifecycle
Track key down and key up consistently, and clear held input when the page loses focus. A missed key-up event can leave a character moving after the player returns to the tab. Touch controls need equivalent actions rather than relying on a keyboard-only workflow.

Bound timing changes
Choose a deliberate timing strategy and handle unusually long frame gaps. A large delta after suspension can move an object through a collision boundary in one update. Test paused tabs and slow devices before deciding whether to clamp elapsed time, use fixed simulation steps, or reset the accumulator on resume.

Design the first useful minute
Tell the player the objective and show the controls before demanding a precise action. Keep retry fast and make win and loss states distinguishable. The supplied game documentation covers several engines and genres; choose one coherent loop instead of combining every available subsystem.

Review restart and cleanup
Start, pause, resume, finish, and restart repeatedly. Check listener counts, timers, audio, and memory growth. Use a small deterministic scenario to reproduce a collision or scoring error. This article is design guidance adapted from the supplied game documentation; the portfolio does not run a game engine.

## Three.js scene lifecycle in a React application
https://codesbyfebin.github.io/blog/grok-build/threejs-react-scene-lifecycle/
Scope: New adaptation of supplied Grok platform documentation: threejs/SKILL.md
Use one dependency strategy
The supplied reference describes a component-based application with package imports. Do not mix an old CDN release, a different installed release, and examples from an unrelated API version. Record the dependency version and check its official documentation before choosing loaders, renderer options, or material APIs.

Treat the scene as an owned resource
A scene integration creates resources such as a canvas, renderer, animation loop, geometries, materials, and textures. Give them a lifecycle owner. React component teardown should stop the loop and detach listeners. Removing a DOM element does not automatically dispose every graphics resource.

Size for the actual container
Use the container's available dimensions when updating the renderer and camera aspect ratio. A full-window assumption fails inside a dashboard panel or responsive card. High device-pixel ratios can increase rendering demand; choose a deliberate budget and compare visual quality with observed performance.

Handle load and failure states
A model or texture request can fail or take longer than expected. Show a useful loading state and a readable fallback. Avoid rendering an empty black panel that suggests the entire interface is broken. The surrounding controls should remain usable while assets load.

Respect the product's interaction model
A decorative scene should not intercept scrolling or keyboard input needed by the page. An interactive scene needs visible controls and an explanation of what the user can do. Provide a static or textual path for content that must remain accessible without a working graphics context.

Verify teardown and remounting
Mount and unmount the scene repeatedly, resize its container, and simulate an asset failure. Inspect whether animation continues after teardown or listeners accumulate. The supplied documentation includes an official Three.js reference pack; this article summarizes integration boundaries without claiming that its examples were rendered or benchmarked.

## A server-side LLM client with explicit cost and failure boundaries
https://codesbyfebin.github.io/blog/grok-build/grok-api-server-side-client/
Scope: New adaptation of supplied Grok platform documentation: xai-api/SKILL.md
Keep credentials behind the server boundary
The supplied platform documentation describes a server-injected model API credential. Read it only in server code and never expose it through a client-prefixed variable, response body, or log. A browser calling your server does not need to know the provider credential.

Validate before spending
A model request can consume the owner's quota. Validate the intended operation, input size, and permission before making the provider call. Public endpoints need a usage policy appropriate to the application. A polished button should not hide an unbounded generation loop or automatic repeat calls.

Choose versions from current documentation
Provider model names, endpoints, and supported features change. The supplied platform snapshot is an integration reference, not a live model catalog. Verify the selected model and request shape against the provider's current official documentation. Record the configuration used for any later measurement.

Treat missing configuration as a real state
When the credential is absent or the backend is unavailable, surface an unavailable state. Do not return a fabricated model answer to keep the interface looking complete. Distinguish configuration failure, request validation failure, timeout, and provider rejection so operators can act on the actual problem.

Streaming needs completion semantics
A stream can contain useful partial output and still fail before the operation finishes. Track completion separately from text arrival. Handle cancellation and client disconnects, and decide what generated artifacts survive. If a response triggers a tool action, validate that action through a separate authorization boundary.

Test the inexpensive paths first
Test missing configuration and invalid input without a provider call. Use an explicit budget for a valid integration check, record the selected model, and preserve the observed response status. This static portfolio makes no model API calls; the guide describes the server-side boundary from the supplied integration documentation.

## A small design system: tokens, states, and accessible composition
https://codesbyfebin.github.io/blog/grok-build/design-system-tokens-accessible-ui/
Scope: New adaptation of supplied Grok platform documentation: design-ui/SKILL.md
Define the vocabulary once
A small design system starts with a palette, type scale, spacing rhythm, radii, and component states. Store these decisions in shared tokens so a theme change updates the whole interface. Repeating unrelated values across components makes visual drift hard to diagnose.

Design around the reader's task
Hierarchy should make the next useful action apparent. An engineering portfolio benefits from readable project boundaries, direct source links, and a connected reading path. Decorative status indicators should not imply that code ran or that a capability was verified.

States are part of the component
A button needs more than a normal appearance. Define focus, disabled, pending, and error behavior where those states apply. A form should preserve the user's input after a recoverable failure. A missing backend should have an explicit unavailable state rather than a permanently spinning loader.

Use contrast and focus deliberately
Check text and controls against their actual backgrounds in each theme. Focus indicators should remain visible for keyboard users. Labels should communicate meaning without depending on color alone. Automated checks can find some issues, but a full accessibility claim needs broader interaction and assistive-technology review.

Compose for narrow screens
Let layouts reduce column count and keep text readable before adding complicated navigation. Code blocks need a bounded horizontal scroll area so they do not widen the entire page. Check long titles, lengthy URLs, and expanded details panels on a narrow viewport.

Motion should support interaction
Use restrained transitions to show relationships or state changes. Respect reduced-motion preferences and avoid continuously animated decoration that competes with reading. The supplied design reference provides a broader system; this guide adapts its token and composition principles without claiming a formal accessibility certification.
